citations.linguistic_note: Exact print birthplace of the 'Newport-Newce' surname-blend hypothesis (Christopher Newport + Sir William Newce) and earliest documented attestation—via hostile refutation—of the oral Tidewater 'ships first seen off that point / news' folk etymology.
citations.analysis_notes: Signing 'H. B. G.' (followed by unsigned/initialed notes in Southern Literary Messenger, Vol. XXX, No. 3, Mar. 1860, p. 209—calling the news story 'a fable... concocted to sustain this last reading'—and Historical Magazine, Vol. V, No. 11, Nov. 1861, p. 348), Virginia antiquarian Hugh Blair Grigsby puts into print a conjecture he later recalled discussing orally around 1828. Grigsby inverts the true orthographic chronology: 17th-century Virginia Company manuscripts (1619–1624) spell the name 'Newportes Newes' / 'Newports News' from the outset, whereas 'Noose' (attested in War of 1812 Craney Island dispatches, e.g. The Military Monitor, July 19, 1813, p. 369) and 'Neuse' are late 18th/19th-century vernacular phonetic spellings reflecting Tidewater /nuːs/.

citations.verbatim_quote: 1 There has been some discussion and considerable research concerning the true orthography of this locality and the origin of its name. The commonly received explanation is that, at one time, when the English colony at Jamestown was in a starving condition, the supply ships of Captain Newport were first seen off this point, and gave the beholders the good news of food at hand; hence the place was called Newport's News. History does not seem to warrant the acceptance of this theory, but furnishes a better. ... A writer in the Historical Magazine (iii. 347) says, that on earlier maps of Virginia, which he has seen, he finds the point called Newport Neuse, which, he argues, is only another way of spelling Newce... Believing that the name was originally a compound of those of Captain Newport and Marshal Newce, the author of this work adopts the orthography given in the text—Newport-Newce.
citations.linguistic_note: Earliest located full book-form statement of the Jamestown 'starving condition / supply ships of Captain Newport / good news of food at hand' folk myth, coinciding with the 1866 post-Civil War U.S. Post Office standardization of 'Newport News'.
citations.analysis_notes: Union occupation of 'Camp Butler, Newport News' in May 1861 thrust the obscure Tidewater headland into national headlines, crystallizing the Starving-Time supply-ship legend in wartime journalism and Lossing's 1866 history. In postal administration, a short-lived first post office established in 1851 (reported in secondary postal tradition as three-word 'New Port News', though Cerinda W. Evans 1947, p. 41 records local 'Newport News' alongside the 1854 U.S. Coast Survey 'Newport News Point') had already disappeared from the 1853 U.S. Official Register and 1857 Leech Post Office Directory (which list only 'Warwick C. H.' in Warwick County); in 1866 the Post Office Department permanently re-established the office as two-word 'Newport News, Warwick, Va.' (verified in the 1870 List of Post Offices, p. 122, and 1870 Official Register).

citations.verbatim_quote: p. 24: 'Indeed, as late as 1864, an eminent writer of the American Antiquarian Society says, "that an antiquarian friend told him that he was passing Newport's News thirty years ago on a steamer, and the old pilot told him that they called it Newport's Noose, and pointed to the cove at the northwest point of land as the noose,"—the very noose that gave name to the place!' | p. 25: 'The misfortune of this narrative is, that there is hardly a word of truth in it. It is, indeed, true, that in 1610 the colonists did leave Jamestown; but, instead of reaching Newport's News, they had gone only as far as Mulberry Island, in the James, a long distance from the place in question; and, instead of meeting Captain Newport, in command of the relieving fleet, they met a longboat from the fleet which was commanded by Sir Thomas West, Lord Delaware, and forthwith returned to Jamestown. Now Newport was really present on this occasion,—which, by the way, happened eleven years before "Newport's News" was named,—but was one of the poor starving colonists himself'
citations.linguistic_note: Landmark antiquarian exchange: (1) records the c. 1834 steamboat-pilot 'Newport's Noose' cove folk etymology (first noted by Charles Deane in AAS Proceedings, Oct. 21, 1864, pp. 71–72n.); (2) refutes the June 1610 De La Warr / Newport legend; (3) exposes Grigsby's reliance on Beverley's 1621 Newport error via Deane's archival footnotes; and (4) directly triggers Gen. citations.analysis_notes: While Grigsby brilliantly demolishes the June 1610 Starving-Time myth on p. 25, his positive fantasy on pp. 26–28—picturing an aged Capt. Thomas Nuse's death is itself dated from 'Newport News'. Nine days after this May 9, 1867 MHS reading, Edward Everett Hale wrote to Deane (May 18, 1867; printed in the Newport News Daily Press, Jan. 17, 1936, and cited in C. W. Evans, VMHB Jan. 1947, pp. 33, 44) proposing 'Newport Ness' (< OE ness 'headland').

Newport's five news-bearing relief voyages (1607–1611, cf. John Smith's 1608 quip 'Newport hath a hundred pounds a yeare for carrying newes') remains the sole morphologically regular explanation.

citations.verbatim_quote: Newport News is referred to sixteen times in the four volumes of the Records of the Virginia Company and the name is spelled in eight different ways: Newportes Newes (4), Newports Newes (4), Newports News (3), Nuports News (1), Newport News (1), Nuport News (1), Newportnews (1), and New ports newes (1). ... The first mention of the name occurs in a document of the Council in Virginia entitled: 'The Putting out of the Tennantes that came over in the B. N. (BONA NOVA), with other orders of the Council', and is dated November 11, 1619... 'are to Choose their divident alonge the banke of the great river betweene Kequohtan and Newportes Newes.'
citations.linguistic_note: Post-1930 foundational scholarship (scan.hosted_path = null): Evans's exhaustive collation of Susan Myra Kingsbury's Records of the Virginia Company of London (4 vols., 1906–1935) establishes the Case 2900 Nov. 11, 1619 baseline and chronologically eliminates Daniel Gookin (Nov. 1621) and Sir William Newce (Oct. 1622).
citations.analysis_notes: Correcting post-1930 popular syntheses that continued to credit Daniel Gookin or the 1610 Starving-Time story (such as the 1940 WPA Virginia: A Guide to the Old Dominion, p. 260, and J. H. R. Yardley's Before the Mayflower, 1931, p. 260), Evans proves five decisive points from Kingsbury's manuscripts: (1) on Nov. 11, 1619 (Records III:227), 'Newportes Newes' was already an established landmark needing no gloss; (2) Capt. Thomas Newce had just landed at Kecoughtan days earlier (Nov. 4, 1619), Daniel Gookin arrived two years later (Nov. 1621), and Sir William Newce did not arrive until October 1622 (Records IV:16, 22, exposing Brown's interpolated '[1621]'); (3) 12 of 16 manuscript spellings mark the genitive '-es/-s' on 'Newport', and all 16 spell the second element 'Newes/News' (never 'Newce/Nuce' or 'Ness'); (4) only 1 of 16 writes 'New ports' as two words; and (5) E. E. Hale's May 18, 1867 'Newport Ness' letter and Gen. B. F. Butler's May 15, 1867 'good news' letter are preserved via their Jan. 17, 1936 Daily Press publication.

citations.analysis_notes: Completes the 19th-to-21st-century historiographical record across two final fronts: (1) when C&O Railway builder Collis P. Huntington began laying out his deepwater coal terminus in Warwick County, his December 6, 1880 bid to replace the historic colonial toponym with 'Minnetta' collapsed under fierce Peninsula resistance prior to the railroad's Oct. 1881 / 1882 opening and the city's Jan. 16, 1896 incorporation; and (2) late-20th-century tertiary/web encyclopedias (mirrored on Wikipedia's 'Newport News, Virginia' entry) introduced two spurious folk-linguistic glosses completely absent from 17th–19th-century Virginia historiography—claiming an unattested Old English word 'news' meaning 'new town' (linguistically impossible: OE niwe tun yields Newton, whereas EModE newes/news is a plural substantivization calquing OFr nouvelles / MedLat nova) or claiming 'New' arose from an original settlement 'rebuilt after a fire' (unattested in colonial records, where Newport News Point was uninhabited by English settlers before 1619–1621).
